### Descriptive Statistics: Summarizing Data

.pull-left[.font90[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("calculator", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Mean (Average)
**S<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** of all values divided by **n<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** of values.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("grip-lines", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Median
**M<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** value when data is ordered from smallest to largest.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("star", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Mode
Most **f<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** occurring value in the dataset.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("arrows-left-right", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Range
Difference between **l<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** and **s<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** values.
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img3, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="55%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p03-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

--

.content-box-green[
.font85[**Answers:** Mean = **sum** &divide; **number** of values &bull; Median = **middle** value &bull; Mode = most **frequently** occurring &bull; Range = **largest** &minus; **smallest**.]
]

---
### Outliers: Values That Stand Out

.pull-left[.font90[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("circle-question", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; What Are Outliers?
Data points much **h<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** or **l<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** than most other values.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("scale-unbalanced", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Why They Matter
Can significantly affect the **m<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** but have less impact on the **m<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>**.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("magnifying-glass", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Identifying Outliers
Look for values **f<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** from the **g<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>l** pattern of data.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("wrench", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Handling Outliers
Investigate **w<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** they exist before deciding whether to **i<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** them.
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img5, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="55%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p05-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

--

.content-box-green[
.font85[**Answers:** much **higher** or **lower** &bull; affect the **mean**, less impact on the **median** &bull; values **far** from the **general** pattern &bull; investigate **why** before deciding whether to **include**.]
]

### Descriptive Statistics Example

.content-box-blue[
**Quiz Scores Dataset:** .font120[{4, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10}]
]

.pull-left[
#### Mean = ?

#### Median = ?

#### Mode = ?

#### Range = ?

#### Possible outlier: ?
]

--

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
**Mean = 8.375** &bull; **Median = 9** &bull; **Mode = 10** &bull; **Range = 6** &bull; **Possible outlier: 4**
]

.font85[
**What this tells us:**

- Average performance around 8&ndash;9 points
- Half scored 9 or above
- Most common score was perfect (10)
- Moderate spread between highest and lowest
- One student struggled significantly more than others
]
]

]

### Clusters and Gaps

.pull-left[
**What to Look For**

.font90[
- **Clusters** show where many data points bunch together, indicating common ranges or typical combinations.

- **Gaps** show ranges with few or no data points, revealing what might be rare or impossible.

- Both help identify **natural groupings** in your data.
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img16, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="95%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p16-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

### Why Finding Patterns Matters

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Make Predictions</strong><br>
  Forecast future outcomes based on past patterns.</div>
</div>

</div>

<div class="chev-row">

</div>

</div>

### Correlation vs. Causation

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("arrows-left-right", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Correlation**

When two variables change together &mdash; as one increases or decreases, so does the other.

*Example: ice cream sales and sunburns both increase on hot days.*

**Just because things happen together doesn't mean one causes the other!**
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
**`r fontawesome::fa("arrow-right", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Causation**

When one event directly results from another &mdash; changing one variable produces a change in the other.

*Example: pushing the gas pedal causes a car to speed up.*

**Proving causation usually requires controlled experiments.**
]
]

---
### Spurious Correlations: Coincidence, Not Causation

.pull-left[.font90[
.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("ice-cream", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Ice Cream and Shark Attacks**

Both increase in summer, but buying ice cream doesn't attract sharks!
]

.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("graduation-cap", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Backpack Weight and Math Scores**

Heavier backpacks correlate with better scores, but weight doesn't cause learning.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("eye-slash", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Hidden Variables**

Often a third factor (like summer weather or study habits) explains both variables.
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img19, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p19-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

### Determining Causation

.pull-left[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Conduct Controlled Experiments</strong><br>
  Randomly assign subjects to treatment and control groups, keeping everything else the same.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Apply Critical Thinking</strong><br>
  Ask if there's a logical reason one variable could influence the other.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Consider Reverse Causation</strong><br>
  Could B actually be causing A instead of A causing B?</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Look for Third Factors</strong><br>
  Could both variables be influenced by something else entirely?</div>
</div>
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img20, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p20-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Inferential Statistics: Beyond Description

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("circle-question", fill = "#4a7fb5")` What Is Inferential Statistics?**

- Making conclusions that go **beyond just describing** your data.
- Helps determine if patterns are **meaningful or just random chance**.
- Uses probability to test hypotheses and make predictions.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("lightbulb", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Example Question**

You try a new study technique and your test score improves.

**Was the technique effective, or did you just happen to get an easier test?**

Inferential statistics helps answer this by measuring how likely the improvement was due to chance.
]
]

---
### Hypotheses: Making Testable Claims

.pull-left[.font90[
.content-box-blue[
**Null Hypothesis (H&#8320;)**

Claims nothing special is happening or there is no effect.

*Example: "The new studying technique has no effect on scores."*
]

.content-box-green[
**Alternative Hypothesis (H&#8321;)**

What you're trying to find evidence for.

*Example: "The new studying technique improves scores."*
]

.content-box-yellow[
**Testing Process**

Collect data and analyze whether it supports the alternative or is consistent with the null.
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img22, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p22-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### P-Values: Measuring Probability

.pull-left[
**What Is a P-Value?**

.font90[
- A number describing how likely your data would occur by **r<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** chance if the null hypothesis were true.

- Small p-value (typically below **0.<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>**) suggests the result is unlikely due to chance.

- Large p-value suggests the result could easily happen by chance.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("coins", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Coin Flip Example**

- Null hypothesis: coin is fair (50% heads)
- You flip 50 times and get 40 heads
- P-value would be **very small** because this outcome is unlikely with a fair coin
- **Conclusion:** reject null hypothesis &mdash; coin is probably biased
]
]

--

.content-box-green[
.font90[**Answers:** by **random** chance; typically below **0.05**.]
]

---
### Statistical Significance

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Set threshold (usually 0.05)</strong><br>
  Decide significance level before analyzing data.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Calculate p-value</strong><br>
  Determine probability of results under null hypothesis.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Compare to threshold</strong><br>
  If p &lt; 0.05, result is statistically significant.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Draw conclusion</strong><br>
  Significant results suggest real effect, not just chance.</div>
</div>

---
### Teaching Methods Example

.content-box-blue[
**The Scenario:** two teaching methods compared with 30 students each. Method A's students scored 5 points higher on average than Method B's. **Question: is this difference meaningful or just random variation?**
]

.pull-left[
**If p-value = 0.01:**

- **B<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** 0.05 threshold
- Statistically **s<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** difference
- Method likely made real impact
]

.pull-right[
**If p-value = 0.3:**

- **A<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** 0.05 threshold
- **N<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>** statistically significant
- Difference might just be **l<u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u>**
]

--

.content-box-green[
.font90[**Answers:** p = 0.01 is **below** the threshold &rarr; statistically **significant**. p = 0.3 is **above** the threshold &rarr; **not** significant; difference might just be **luck**.]
]

---
class: segue-yellow

# SHIFTING FOCUS: <br> Parts of a Research Report `r top_icon("book-open")`

---
### Literature Review *(Refresher)*

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
A literature review is a **summary and analysis** of what has already been written on a topic.
]

**It helps you:**

.font90[
- Understand what's already known,
- See where there are gaps or debates,
- Avoid repeating others' work,
- And build a strong foundation for your own research.
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img28, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p28-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### How to Conduct a Lit Review *(Refresher)*

.font85[
<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Clarify Your Topic or Research Question</strong></div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Search for Reliable Sources</strong></div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Skim and Select</strong> &mdash; read abstracts first; choose a mix of recent, relevant, and diverse perspectives; aim for at least 5&ndash;10 solid sources.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Take Notes</strong> &mdash; write down the main point of each source; note how it relates to your topic; use color coding or a chart to organize themes.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">5</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Group by Themes or Ideas</strong> &mdash; don't stop at summarizing each article one by one. Instead, group your notes by common <strong><u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u></strong>, <strong><u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u></strong>, or <strong><u>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</u></strong>.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">6</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Start Writing</strong></div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row-sm">
  <div class="chev-sm">7</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Cite Everything</strong></div>
</div>
]

.content-box-green[
.font90[**Step 5 answers:** group your notes by common **themes**, **disagreements**, or **trends**.]
]

<br>

### Academic Writing Characteristics

.font80[
.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("user-tie", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Formal Tone**

Professional language without slang or contractions. "A survey was conducted" rather than "I asked my friends."
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("scale-balanced", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Objective Focus**

Emphasizes evidence over opinion. "The data suggest..." instead of "I think..."
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("list-check", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Thorough Detail**

Provides enough information for others to replicate your work or evaluate your methods.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("quote-right", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Proper Citations**

Acknowledges all sources using standard formats like APA, MLA, or Chicago style.
]
]
]

---
### Literature Review Template

.pull-left[.font85[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("flag", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Begin with a short introduction**

What is your topic? Why is it important? Give the broad context of the problem.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("paragraph", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Body**

Share what other studies have found. Organize the body **by themes, not by author**.
]

.content-box-green[
**`r fontawesome::fa("flag-checkered", fill = "#4a7fb5")` End with a summary**

Summarize what was found. Clarify how your project connects to past research. Name the patterns you noticed in the literature. Identify the gaps and/or questions that remain to be explored.
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img36, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p28-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### How to Synthesize Multiple Sources in a Lit Review

.content-box-blue[
**What does synthesis mean?**

A good lit review is **more than just summarizing** what you found. It means **combining ideas from different sources** to see how they relate to each other, not just what each one says.
]

--

.font85[
**`r fontawesome::fa("link", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Look for Connections** &mdash; ask yourself: do the authors agree or disagree? Are they studying the same issue from different perspectives? Does one source support, expand on, or challenge another?

**`r fontawesome::fa("layer-group", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Group Ideas, Not Authors** &mdash; don't organize your review by author: "Smith says..., then Jones says..." Instead, organize by theme, issue, or trend. *Example: "Many studies agree that social media affects attention span (Smith, 2021; Lee, 2020), but a few challenge this idea (Gomez, 2022)."*
]

---
### How to Synthesize Multiple Sources (continued)

.font85[
**`r fontawesome::fa("comments", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Use Comparative Language** &mdash; helpful phrases: *"Similarly..."* &bull; *"In contrast..."* &bull; *"Building on..."* &bull; *"While some researchers argue..., others suggest..."* &bull; *"There is a general consensus that..."*

**`r fontawesome::fa("magnifying-glass", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Highlight Gaps or Conflicts** &mdash; point out where sources disagree or where more research is needed. *Example: "While most studies link sleep to better memory, few explore how this differs by age group."*

**`r fontawesome::fa("mountain-sun", fill = "#4a7fb5")` End With a Big Picture** &mdash; what have you learned from all the sources combined? What patterns, debates, or gaps have you noticed? This sets the stage for your own research question.
]

---
### Importance of Giving Reference *(Refresher)*

.content-box-blue[
**Why Do We Cite?**

Citing your sources means **giving credit** to the original authors of the ideas, words, or data you use in your work.
]

--

**We cite to:**

#### `r fontawesome::fa("user-shield", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Avoid plagiarism (taking credit for someone else's work)

#### `r fontawesome::fa("map-pin", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Show where your information came from

#### `r fontawesome::fa("magnifying-glass", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Help others find those sources if they want to learn more

---
### What to Cite? What Not to Cite? *(Refresher)*

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("check", fill = "#009E73")` You should cite:**

- Direct quotes (even short ones)
- Paraphrased ideas (putting someone else's idea into your own words)
- Statistics or data
- Images, charts, or graphics you didn't create
]
]

--

.pull-right[
.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("xmark", fill = "#D55E00")` You do not need to cite:**

- Common knowledge (e.g., "Water freezes at 0&deg;C")
- Your own original thoughts
]
]

---
### How to Cite?

.font85[
There are different citation styles (**APA, MLA, Chicago**), but the basic idea is the same: you include the author's name, date, and sometimes the page number in your text, and then list the full details at the end of your work.

.content-box-blue[
**Example in APA Style:**

**In-text citation:** "Teens who sleep less are more likely to report symptoms of depression" (Williams, 2021, p. 45).

**Works Cited/References page:** Williams, A. (2021). *The Science of Teen Sleep.* TeenHealth Publishing.
]

.content-box-yellow[
**When citing online resources**, instead of writing just a link, include full source info:

**Not this:** https://example.com/article

**Do this:** Smith, J. (2022). Climate change and food security. *National Environmental Journal.* https://example.com/article
]
]

---
### Tips for Citations

#### `r fontawesome::fa("table-list", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Keep track of your sources as you research (write down author, title, date, and link)

#### `r fontawesome::fa("clock", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Don't wait until the end to cite; build it in as you go

#### `r fontawesome::fa("wand-magic-sparkles", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Use citation tools (like EasyBib, Zotero, or the built-in Google Docs citation feature) to help format correctly

#### `r fontawesome::fa("circle-check", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Always double-check your citations with your teacher's required style guide

--

.content-box-blue[
**Closing thought:** citing is part of being a **trustworthy researcher**. It shows you're respectful of other people's work and serious about your own.
]

---

### Comparing Two Groups: The t-Test

.pull-left[.font90[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("bullseye", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Purpose
Compares means of two groups to see if they're significantly different.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("calculator", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Calculation Factors
Considers difference between means, variability within groups, and sample size.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("square-poll-vertical", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Results
Produces t-statistic and p-value to determine significance.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("flask", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Common Uses
Testing new methods, comparing treatments, evaluating interventions.
]]

.pull-right[

### t-Test Example: Learning App Study

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**The Scenario**

- Class A tried a new learning app for a month
- Class B used traditional homework
- Class A mean score: **85**
- Class B mean score: **80**

**Question:** Is the 5-point difference due to the app or just chance?
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img52, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="85%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p52-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

--

.content-box-green[
.font90[**t-statistic: 3.59** &bull; **p-value: 0.0009** &bull; Result: statistically significant (p &lt; 0.05) &bull; **Conclusion: the app likely had a positive effect on scores.**]
]

### Regression Analysis: Finding Relationships

.pull-left[
**What Is Regression?**

.font90[
- A method to **model or predict** one variable based on another.

- Finds the **"line of best fit"** through data points.

- Quantifies the relationship between variables.
]

.content-box-blue[
.font90[**Example:** predicting test scores based on study hours. The upward slope shows more study time relates to higher scores.]
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img53, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="92%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p53-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Linear Regression Equation

.pull-left[
.font130[$$Y = a + bX$$]

.font90[
- **Y** is the predicted value, **X** is the independent variable

- **a** is the intercept &mdash; where the line crosses the y-axis (Y when X=0)

- **b** is the slope &mdash; how much Y changes when X increases by one unit
]
]

.pull-right[
```{r img54, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p54-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Regression Example: Study Hours vs. Test Scores

.pull-left[
```{r img55, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p55-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font85[
.content-box-blue[
**Regression equation:** Score = 50 + 5&times;(Hours)
]

- **Interpretation:** each additional hour studied is associated with an increase of **5 points** on the test, on average.

- **Prediction:** a student studying 8 hours would score about 50 + 5&times;8 = **90 points**.

- X = study hours; Y = test score. Intercept (50) is what Y is when X is 0; slope (5) is how much Y changes when X increases by one unit.
]]

### Important Regression Concepts

.three-col[
.col[
`r fontawesome::fa("arrows-up-down", height = "2em", fill = "#4a7fb5")`

**Residuals**

.font85[Differences between actual values and predicted values. Smaller residuals mean better fit.]
]
.col[
`r fontawesome::fa("percent", height = "2em", fill = "#4a7fb5")`

**R-squared**

.font85[Number between 0 and 1 showing how much variation in Y is explained by X. Higher is better.]
]
.col[
`r fontawesome::fa("arrows-left-right-to-line", height = "2em", fill = "#4a7fb5")`

**Interpolation vs. Extrapolation**

.font85[Predicting within observed range (safer) vs. outside that range (riskier).]
]
]

---
### Quasi-Experimental Designs

.pull-left[.font90[
.content-box-blue[
When true experiments aren't possible, researchers use clever statistical designs to **approximate experiments using observational data**.
]

#### `r fontawesome::fa("triangle-exclamation", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Selection Bias Challenge
Groups receiving treatment may differ in other ways that affect outcomes.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("bullseye", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Goal
Find ways to estimate cause-and-effect without random assignment.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("gears", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Methods
Special techniques help address selection bias and isolate treatment effects.
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img57, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p57-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Difference-in-Differences (DID)

.pull-left[.font90[
**How It Works**

- Compare changes over time between a treatment group and a control group.

- Calculate: **(After &minus; Before for Treatment) &minus; (After &minus; Before for Control)**

- This removes common factors affecting both groups, isolating the treatment effect.

.content-box-green[
- Group A (with program): 70 &rarr; 78 (**+8**)
- Group B (no program): 68 &rarr; 70 (**+2**)
- Difference-in-differences: +8 &minus; +2 = **+6 points**
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img58, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="92%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p58-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Regression Discontinuity (RD)

.pull-left[.font90[
**How It Works**

- Takes advantage of a **sharp cutoff** for treatment assignment.

- Compares outcomes for subjects just below and just above the cutoff.

- These subjects should be very similar except for receiving treatment.

.content-box-blue[
**Example:** students scoring below 50 get special tutoring. Compare students who scored 49 vs. 51 &mdash; practically the same ability, but different treatment. Any jump in outcomes at the cutoff suggests a **causal effect**.
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img59, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="92%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p59-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

---
### Instrumental Variables (IV)

.pull-left[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Find an Instrument (Z)</strong><br>
  Something that affects X but not Y directly.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Isolate Variation</strong><br>
  Use only the variation in X caused by Z.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Measure Effect</strong><br>
  See how this "clean" variation affects Y.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Draw Conclusions</strong><br>
  Estimate causal impact of X on Y.</div>
</div>
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img60, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="52%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/p60-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

### Matching: Creating Comparable Groups

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**How It Works**

- Match each treated subject with similar non-treated subjects.
- Compare outcomes between matched pairs.
- Creates balanced groups *as if* in an experiment.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
**Example**

For each student in a tutoring program, find another student with:

- Similar initial grades
- Similar background
- Similar motivation level

Compare outcomes between matched pairs to estimate the tutoring effect.
]
]
